en: Having placed the Lord of All within my heart and performed obeisance to my guru,
this *Tarkasaṃgraha* is composed for the easy understanding of beginners.
Substance, quality, action, generality, particularity, inherence, and absence—these are the seven categories.
In that regard, substances are exactly nine: earth, water, fire, air, ether, time, space, self, and mind.

The twenty-four qualities (guṇas) are: color, taste, smell, touch, number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, gravity, fluidity, viscidity, sound, cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, merit, demerit, and mental impression.
Throwing upward, throwing downward, contraction, expansion, and going—these are the five types of action.
Generality is of two kinds: the higher and the lower.
The ultimate particulars (viśeṣas), however, which reside in eternal substances, are indeed infinite.
Inherence, however, is only one.
Non-existence is of four kinds:
antecedent non-existence, non-existence through destruction, absolute non-existence, and mutual non-existence.
The earth possessing fragrance is of two kinds: eternal and non-eternal. That which is eternal exists in the form of atoms.
It is impermanent and of the nature of an effect;
furthermore, it is threefold due to the distinction between body, sense-faculties, and objects.
The body belongs to those such as ourselves.
The faculty that perceives odor is the nose, which is located at the tip of the nose;
its object consists of earth, stone, and so forth.
Water possesses the quality of cold touch;
it is of two kinds: eternal and non-eternal. The eternal [water] exists in the form of atoms (*paramāṇu*).
They are impermanent and of the nature of effects.
Furthermore, they are of three kinds, distinguished as body, sense faculty, and object.
The body [exists] in the world of Varuṇa.
The sense faculty is the tongue, which perceives taste and resides at the tip of the tongue;
its object consists of rivers, oceans, and so forth.
Fire has the characteristic of hot touch.
It is of two kinds: eternal and non-eternal. The eternal is that which exists in the form of atoms.
The impermanent consists of the nature of effects;
furthermore, it is threefold through the distinction of body, sense-faculties, and objects.
The body exists in the world of the sun.
The sense faculty that apprehends visible form is the eye, located at the tip of the black pupil. Its objects are of four kinds, distinguished as terrestrial, celestial, gastric, and mineral.
Terrestrial fire consists of fire and so forth; celestial fire, which has no fuel, consists of lightning and so forth;
the digestive fire is the cause of the transformation of what has been eaten; and mine-born fire consists of gold and the like.
Wind is that which is devoid of form and possesses tangibility.
It is of two kinds: eternal and non-eternal. The eternal is in the form of atoms.
It is impermanent and of the nature of an effect.
Furthermore, it is threefold, distinguished as body, sense organ, and object.
The body exists in the world of wind.
The faculty is the skin, which perceives touch and pervades the entire body;
its object is the cause of the trembling of trees and so forth.
The wind that moves within the body is *prāṇa*;
although it is one, it receives the designations of *prāṇa*, *apāna*, and so forth due to the distinction of its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).
Space has sound as its quality;
it is one, all-pervading, and eternal.
Time is the cause of the conventional designations of "past" and so forth; it is one, all-pervading, and eternal.
Space is the cause of the conventional usage of "east" and so forth;
it is one, all-pervading, and eternal.
The substratum of knowledge is the self (ātman).
It is of two kinds: the supreme self (paramātman) and the individual self (jīvātman). Among these, the Lord (īśvara), who is omniscient, is the one and only supreme self.
The individual self (jīvātman) is distinct in each body, all-pervading, and eternal.
The internal organ (*manas*) is the sense-faculty that effects the apprehension of pleasure and so forth;
and because it is restricted to each individual self, it is infinite, atomic in form, and eternal.
Color (*rūpa*) is a quality (*guṇa*) perceivable by the eye alone.
It is of seven kinds, distinguished as white, blue, yellow, red, green, brown, and variegated; it resides in earth, water, and fire.
Among these, all seven kinds reside in earth.
Luminous white resides in water;
radiant white resides in fire.
Taste is a quality perceivable by the tongue;
it is of six kinds, distinguished as sweet, sour, salty, pungent, astringent, and bitter.
It exists in all six varieties within the earth element.
In water, it is indeed sweet.
Odor is the quality apprehended by the sense of smell;
it is of two kinds, namely, fragrant and foul,
and it exists only in earth.
Tangible quality (*sparśa*) is a property perceivable solely by the tactile faculty (*tvagindriya*).
It is of three kinds, distinguished as cold, hot, and neither-hot-nor-cold.
It subsists in earth, water, fire, and air.
In that regard, coldness is in water; heat is in fire;
and that which is neither hot nor cold is in earth and air.
The fourfold set beginning with form (*rūpa*) is produced by maturation (*pākaja*) and is impermanent in earth; elsewhere it is not produced by maturation, is permanent, and is ultimate.
That which resides in the permanent is permanent.
That which belongs to the impermanent is impermanent.
Number is the cause for the linguistic usage of "oneness" and so forth.
It resides in the nine substances and ranges from oneness up to the highest number (parārdha).
Oneness is both eternal and non-eternal.
That which belongs to the eternal is eternal; that which belongs to the non-eternal is non-eternal;
however, duality and so forth are invariably non-eternal in all cases.
Dimension (parimāṇa) is the cause for human transactions;
it resides in nine substances and is of four kinds.
Minute, large, long, and short.
Separateness (*pṛthaktva*) is the cause for the conventional usage of "distinct";
it resides in all substances.
Conjunction is the cause of the conventional usage of "conjoined";
it resides in all substances.
Disjunction is the quality that causes the destruction of conjunction;
it resides in all substances.
Remoteness (*paratva*) and proximity (*aparatva*) are the uncommon causes for the conventional designations "remote" and "proximate.
They reside in the four elements beginning with earth, as well as in the mind (*manas*).
These two are of two kinds: produced by direction (*dikkṛta*) and produced by time (*kālakṛta*).
Remoteness caused by direction exists in that which is situated at a distance; nearness caused by direction exists in that which is situated nearby;
remoteness caused by time exists in that which is elder.
In the case of the youngest, inferiority is determined by age.
Gravity is the non-inherent cause of the first fall;
it resides in earth and water.
Fluidity (*dravatva*), which is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) of the first [type of] motion (*ādyasyandana*), resides in earth, water, and fire.
It is of two kinds: natural (*sāṃsiddhika*) and incidental (*naimittika*). Natural fluidity exists in water; incidental fluidity exists in earth and fire.
In earth, such as in ghee and the like, there is fluidity produced by conjunction with fire; in fire, such as in gold and the like, it is natural.
Stickiness (*sneha*) is the quality that causes powdered substances and the like to coalesce into a mass;
it resides exclusively in water.
Sound is a quality perceivable by the ear; it exists only in space (*ākāśa*). It is of two kinds: consisting of substance (*dravyātmaka*) and consisting of phonemes (*varṇātmaka*).
That which consists of substance exists in things such as drums;
that which consists of phonemes takes the form of the Sanskrit language and so forth.
In the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* (AnTs 34), it is stated: "Intellect (*buddhi*) is knowledge (*jñāna*), which is the cause of all worldly transactions.
It is of two kinds: memory (*smṛti*) and experience (*anubhava*).
Knowledge produced solely by mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) is memory."
Cognition distinct from that is experience.

That [cognition] is of two kinds: valid (yathārtha) and invalid (ayathārtha). A valid cognition is an experience that possesses a qualifier in that which bears it; for example, the cognition "this is silver" with respect to silver.
That alone is called valid cognition (*pramā*).
An experience that has a particular feature as its qualifier when that feature is absent is invalid (*ayathārtha*),
such as the cognition "this is silver" with respect to mother-of-pearl.
Valid experience of reality as it is (yathārthānubhava) is fourfold, distinguished as perception (pratyakṣa), inference (anumiti), comparison (upamiti), and verbal testimony (śabda).
Its instruments (tatkaraṇa) are likewise fourfold, distinguished as perception (pratyakṣa), inference (anumāna), comparison (upamāna), and verbal testimony (śabda).

AnTs_37: A cause that is not common [to other effects] is an instrument (*karaṇa*). AnTs_38: A cause is that which invariably precedes its effect. AnTs_39: An effect is that which has prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) as its counter-positive.

The cause is threefold, distinguished as the inherent (samavāyi), the non-inherent (asamavāyi), and the instrumental (nimitta). That in which the effect inheres when it is produced is the inherent cause;
for example, threads are the inherent cause of cloth, and cloth is the inherent cause of the color and other qualities residing in the sky.
When a cause exists in a state of inherence within the same object as either the effect or another cause, that cause is an *asamavāyikāraṇa* (non-inherent cause).
For example, the conjunction of threads is the non-inherent cause of a cloth, and the color of the threads is the non-inherent cause of the color of the cloth.
A cause distinct from both of these is a *nimittakāraṇa* (instrumental cause).
Just as the shuttle, the loom, and so forth are for a cloth;
among these three kinds of causes, that which is the uncommon cause is alone the instrument (*karaṇa*).
In that context, perception is the instrument for perceptual knowledge.
Knowledge produced by the contact of a sense faculty with its object is perception.
It is of two kinds: non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) and conceptual (*savikalpaka*).

In this context, non-conceptual knowledge (*nirvikalpaka-jñāna*) is that which is free from conceptual construction, such as "this is something. Conceptual knowledge (*savikalpaka-jñāna*) is that which possesses qualifiers, such as "This is Ditttha," "This is a Brahmin," or "This is dark-complexioned."
The cause of perceptual knowledge is the contact between the sense organ and its object, which is of six kinds:

conjunction (*saṃyoga*), inherence in the conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavāya*), inherence in what is inherent in the conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavetasamavāya*), inherence (*samavāya*), inherence in the inherent (*samavetasamavāya*), and the relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*).
In the production of the perception of a jar by means of the eye, conjunction is the contact.

In the production of the perception of the color of a jar, the sense-object contact is *saṃyuktasamavāya* (inherence in what is conjoined), because color inheres in the jar which is conjoined with the eye.

In the perception of the generality "color-ness," the contact is *saṃyuktasamavetasamavāya* (inherence in what inheres in what is conjoined), because the jar is conjoined with the eye, color inheres in it, and "color-ness" inheres therein. In the case of sound and the auditory organ, since sound is a quality of space (*ākāśa*), and because there is inherence between a quality and its possessor, the contact is likewise [of that nature].
In the direct perception of "sound-ness" (śabdatva), the contact is inherence-in-the-inherent (samavetasamavāya), because sound-ness inheres in the sound which is inherent in the auditory organ.

In the perception of absence (abhāva), the contact is the qualifier-qualified relation (viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva), as in the case of "the ground is devoid of a jar," where the absence of the jar is the qualifier of the ground with which the eye is in contact.
Thus, perception is cognition produced by the six types of proximity;
its instrument is the sense faculty.
Therefore, it is established that the sense faculty is the means of valid perception (*pratyakṣapramāṇa*).
Inference is the instrument of inferential cognition.

Inferential cognition is a knowledge produced by a subsumptive reflection (*parāmarśa*). Subsumptive reflection is the knowledge of the presence of the reason in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) as qualified by pervasion (*vyāpti*).
For example, the cognition "this mountain possesses smoke which is pervaded by fire" is *parāmarśa* (reflective judgment).
The cognition produced by that, namely "the mountain possesses fire," is *anumiti* (inference).
The rule of concomitance, "wherever there is smoke, there is fire," is *vyāpti* (pervasion).
The property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) is the occurrence of the pervaded (*vyāpya*) in the mountain and so forth.
Inference is of two kinds: for oneself (*svārtha*) and for others (*parārtha*).
Among these, that which is for oneself is the cause of one's own inferential cognition.
For instance, by means of repeated observation oneself—such as in a kitchen and so forth—one perceives the pervasion (*vyāpti*) that "wherever there is smoke, there is fire."

Having taken [the fire] and gone near the mountain, when the fire has departed, one who is in doubt yet perceives smoke on the mountain remembers the pervasion (*vyāpti*): "Wherever there is smoke, there is fire. Immediately thereafter, the cognition arises: "This mountain possesses smoke which is pervaded by fire."
This very process is called the consideration of the logical mark (liṅgaparāmarśa). From that, the inferential cognition "the mountain possesses fire" arises;
this is inference for oneself (svārthānumāna).
However, when one, having personally inferred fire from smoke, employs a five-membered syllogistic statement for the sake of another's understanding, that is inference for others (*parārthānumāna*).
For example: "The mountain possesses fire because it possesses smoke;
whatever possesses smoke possesses fire, as in the case of a kitchen."
And so it is with this [person]: "Therefore, it is thus.
By means of this, another person also understands fire from the indicated mark (*liṅga*).
The five members [of a syllogism] are the proposition, the reason, the example, the application, and the conclusion.
"The mountain possesses fire" is the proposition.
"Because it possesses smoke" is the reason.
"Whatever possesses smoke possesses fire, as in a kitchen"—this is the example (*udāharaṇa*). "And so is this [mountain]"—this is the application (*upanaya*).
"Therefore, it is so"—this is the conclusion (*nigamana*).
In both inference for oneself (*svārthānumiti*) and inference for others (*parārthānumiti*), the consideration of the logical mark (*liṅgaparāmarśa*) alone is the instrument.
Therefore, inference is the consideration of the logical mark.
The logical mark (liṅga) is of three kinds:

positive-and-negative (anvayavyatireki), purely positive (kevalānvayi), and purely negative (kevalavyatireki). That which possesses pervasion (vyāpti) through both positive and negative concomitance is the positive-and-negative.
For example, when fire is the probandum, "possessing smoke" is the reason;

where there is smoke, there is fire, as in a kitchen—this is positive concomitance (anvayavyāpti). Where fire is absent, smoke is also absent, as in a great lake—this is negative concomitance (vyatirekavyāpti).
The purely positive inference (*kevalānvayi*) has only positive concomitance (*anvaya-vyāpti*), as for example: "A jar is nameable (*abhidheya*) because it is knowable (*prameya*), like a cloth.
Here, there is no negative concomitance (*vyatireka-vyāpti*) between knowability and nameability, because everything is both knowable and nameable.
The purely negative inference (*kevalavyatireki*) has only negative concomitance, as for example: "Earth is distinct from the others [elements] because it possesses odor."
That which does not differ from others is not possessed of odor,
like water;
and this [earth] is not like that.

Therefore, regarding the statement "it is not so," there is no positive instance (*anvaya-dṛṣṭānta*) for the proposition "whatever possesses odor is distinct from others," because the earth alone constitutes the subject (*pakṣa*).
The subject (pakṣa) is that which possesses a probandum (sādhya) that is still in doubt;
for example, a mountain when "possessing smoke" is the reason (hetu).
The similar instance (sapakṣa) is that which possesses the property to be proven as a certainty; for example, in that very same case, the kitchen.
The *vipakṣa* (dissimilar instance) is that which possesses the definitely ascertained absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*);
for example, in that very same case, a large lake.

AnTs_52 The five fallacious reasons (hetvābhāsa) are: the erratic (savyabhicāra), the contradictory (viruddha), the one whose locus is doubtful (satpratipakṣa), the unestablished (asiddha), and the sublated (bādhita).

The *savyabhicāra* (inconclusive) reason is that which is *anaikāntika* (uncertain). It is of three kinds, distinguished as *sādhāraṇa* (common), *asādhāraṇa* (uncommon), and *anupasamhārī* (non-conclusive).
Among these, the inconclusive (anaikāntika) reason that resides in that which lacks the probandum (sādhyābhāvavat) is the common (sādhāraṇa).
For example, in the inference "The mountain possesses fire because it is cognizable" (prameyatvāt), the property of being cognizable exists in a lake, which lacks fire.
The uncommon (asādhāraṇa) reason is that which is excluded from all similar instances (sapakṣa) and dissimilar instances (vipakṣa).
For example: "Sound is eternal because it possesses the nature of sound" (*śabdatva*).
Here, the property of being sound (*śabdatva*) is excluded from all eternal things and from all ultimate particulars (*antyaviśeṣa*), and it subsists in sound alone.
This is a non-conclusive reason (*anupasamhārī*) that lacks both positive and negative examples.
For example: "Everything is impermanent because it is an object of cognition.
Here, since everything is included within the subject (*pakṣa*), there is no corroborative instance (*dṛṣṭānta*).

A contradictory reason (*viruddha*) is one that is pervaded by the absence of the property to be proven (*sādhyābhāva*). For example, in the case where "sound is eternal because it is produced," the state of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) is indeed pervaded by non-eternality, which is the absence of eternality.
An *satpratipakṣa* (counter-balanced) reason is that for which there exists another reason (*hetvantara*) that establishes the opposite of the state to be proven (*sādhyabhāva*).
For example: "Sound is eternal, because it is audible, like the nature of sound (*śabdatva*)," and "Sound is non-eternal, because it is a product, like a jar."
The unestablished (asiddha) is of three kinds:
the unestablished in its locus (āśrayāsiddha), the unestablished in its own nature (svarūpāsiddha), and the unestablished in its pervasion (vyāpyatvāsiddha).
The unestablished in its locus is, for example: "A sky-lotus is fragrant because it is a lotus, like a pond-lotus."
In this case, the sky-lotus is the locus, and that simply does not exist.
An example of a reason whose essential nature is unestablished (*svarūpāsiddha*) is: "Sound is a quality because it is visible."
And here, visibility does not exist in sound, because sound is audible.

This is a case of unestablished pervasion (*vyāpyatvāsiddha*) due to a limiting condition (*upādhi*). A limiting condition is that which, while pervading the probandum (*sādhya*), does not pervade the probans (*sādhana*).

Pervasion of the probandum (*sādhyavyāpakatva*) consists in not being the counter-positive of an absolute absence that is co-locus with the probandum. Non-pervasion of the locus of the probans (*sādhanāvyāpakatva*) consists in being the counter-positive of an absolute absence that is admitted to exist in what possesses the probans. In the inference "The mountain possesses smoke because it possesses fire," the conjunction with wet fuel (*ārdrendhana-saṃyoga*) is the limiting condition (*upādhi*).
For instance:

"Where there is smoke, there is contact with moist fuel"—this is pervasion by the probandum (*sādhyavyāpakatā*). "Where there is fire, there is an absence of contact with moist fuel"—this is non-pervasion by the probans (*sādhanāvyāpakatā*).
Thus, because it pervades the probandum while not pervading the probans, contact with wet fuel is an *upādhi*;
due to this possession of an *upādhi*, the state of possessing fire is unestablished as being pervaded (*vyāpyatvāsiddha*).
An argument whose absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*) is ascertained by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is "sublated" (*bādhita*).
For example: "Fire is not hot, because it is a substance.
Here, the probandum is "not being hot," and its absence—namely, "being hot"—is apprehended through tactile perception; thus, the argument is sublated.
Comparison (*upamāna*) is the instrument for comparison (*upamiti*). Comparison is the knowledge of the relationship between a name and the object named;
its instrument is the knowledge of similarity.

The recollection of the meaning of the analogical statement (*atideśavākya*) is the intermediate operation. For instance, someone who does not know the referent of the word "gavaya" hears from a forest-dweller that "a gavaya is like a cow," and having gone to the forest while recollecting the meaning of that statement, he perceives an individual object resembling a cow.
Immediately after that, the analogical cognition arises: "This is what is denoted by the word 'gavaya'."
Verbal testimony (śabda) is the statement of a reliable person (āpta-vākya). A reliable person, however, is one who speaks in accordance with reality.
A statement is a collection of words.

For example, in the command "Bring the cow," the word "cow" possesses a capacity (*śakti*). This capacity is the convention (*saṃketa*) established by God that "this meaning is to be understood from this word."
Expectancy (ākāṅkṣā), semantic competency (yogyatā), and contiguity (saṃnidhi) are the causes for the knowledge of the meaning of a sentence.
Expectancy is a word’s lack of capacity to produce the cognition of a syntactic connection when another word is absent.
Semantic competency is the non-sublation of the meaning.
Proximity (*saṃnidhi*) is the utterance of words without delay.
A sentence devoid of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and the other [conditions] is not a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*).
For example, "cow, horse, man, elephant" is not a means of valid cognition due to the absence of expectancy.
"One should sprinkle with fire" is not a means of valid cognition due to the absence of compatibility (*yogyatā*).
Words such as "bring the cow," uttered at every single moment, are not a means of valid cognition due to the absence of proximity (saṃnidhi).
Speech is of two kinds:
Vedic and worldly.
Because it was spoken by God, all Vedic speech is indeed authoritative.
However, in the worldly context, that which is spoken by a reliable person is authoritative;
anything else is not authoritative.
The knowledge of the meaning of a sentence is the knowledge of the word;
the word is the instrument for that [knowledge].
Invalid experience (ayathārthānubhava) is threefold, distinguished by the categories of doubt (saṃśaya), error (viparyaya), and uncertainty (tarka).
Doubt is a cognition that apprehends the presence of various contradictory properties in a single substratum (dharmin);
for example, "Is it a post or a person?"
False knowledge is error, such as [the cognition] "this is silver" with respect to mother-of-pearl.

Hypothetical reasoning (*tarka*) is the attribution of a pervader (*vyāpaka*) through the attribution of a pervaded (*vyāpya*), such as: "If fire were not present, then smoke would also not be present."
Recollection (*smṛti*) is also of two kinds:

that which corresponds to reality and that which does not correspond to reality. That which is produced by valid cognition (*pramā*) corresponds to reality; that which is produced by non-valid cognition (*apramā*) does not correspond to reality.
Happiness is that which is to be experienced as agreeable by all.
Suffering is that which is to be experienced as disagreeable by all.
Desire is longing.
Anger is hatred.
An effort is an exertion.
Dharma is that which is produced by enjoined action.
Adharma, however, is that which is produced by prohibited actions.
The eight beginning with cognition (buddhi) are the specific qualities belonging solely to the self (ātman).
Intellect, desire, and effort are of two kinds:
eternal and non-eternal.
The eternal ones belong to the Lord (Īśvara).
The life-force is impermanent.
Formative forces (*saṃskāra*) are of three kinds:
momentum (*vega*), mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*), and elasticity (*sthitisthāpaka*).
Momentum is a function of the four elements beginning with earth, as well as of the mind.
Latent disposition (*bhāvanā*) is that which arises from experience, serves as the cause of memory, and resides solely in the self (*ātman*).
Elasticity (*sthitisthāpaka*), on the other hand, is that which restores to its original state what has been altered; it resides in earth, such as mats and the like.
Action is of the nature of motion.
Throwing upward is the cause of conjunction with an upper location;
throwing downward is the cause of conjunction with a lower location.
Contraction is the cause of conjunction with what is proximate to the body;
extension is the cause of conjunction with what is remote;
everything else is locomotion.
The fourfold [elements] beginning with earth function solely within the mind.
Generality (*sāmānya*) is eternal, unitary, and inherent in many individuals;
it resides in substances, qualities, and actions.
It is of two kinds, distinguished as the higher (*para*) and the lower (*apara*).
The higher [genus] is existence (sattā);
the lower [genus] is substantiality (dravyatva) and so forth.
Particularities (*viśeṣa*) are those factors residing in eternal substances that serve to differentiate them.

Inherence (samavāya) is an eternal relation; it exists between things that are inseparably established (ayutasiddha). Those two among a pair of things, one of which, without perishing, remains necessarily dependent upon the other, are said to be inseparably established.

Just as, for example, the part and the whole, the quality and the possessor of quality, the action and the agent of action, the universal and the individual, and the particular and the eternal substance.
Prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is beginningless but has an end;
it pertains to an effect prior to its production. Destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*) has a beginning but is endless.
After the production [of a thing],
there is absolute non-existence (atyantābhāva) whose counter-correlativity (pratiyogitā) is delimited by a relation existing across the three periods of time;
for example, "there is no jar on the ground."
Mutual absence (anyonyābhāva) is that whose counter-positiveness is delimited by the relation of identity (tādātmya), as for example: "A pot is not a cloth."
Since all categories are included, as appropriate, within those already mentioned, it is established that there are exactly seven categories.
The *Tarkasaṃgraha* has been composed by the learned Annambhaṭṭa for the sake of establishing the proficiency of beginners in the systems of Kaṇāda and Nyāya.
